did_you_know.text: Did you know? The Israelites reached the Wilderness of Sin on the fifteenth day of the second month—about one month after the Exodus, which began on the fifteenth of Nisan.
Did you know? “The Wilderness of Sin” is the name of a geographic region and is not related to the word “sin.” Its exact location is unknown today.
Did you know? In their complaint, the Israelites describe Egypt as a time of plenty and security, although the Torah also describes harsh slavery there. Memories of the past are not always accurate.

Did you know? The phrase “a day’s portion day by day” expresses the idea of taking what is needed for each day rather than storing everything in advance. The test involves both trust and responsible action.
Did you know? Quail are migratory birds, and flocks of them pass through desert regions during certain seasons. Such birds may land when exhausted after a long flight.
Did you know? The word “manna” is explained in the verse as a question: “What is it?” This is also the source of the word manna in many languages.
Did you know? An omer was an ancient measure of volume, not a fixed modern weight. That is why it is difficult to convert it precisely into liters.

Did you know? The story distinguishes between how much people gathered and how much food each person ended up with: some gathered much and others little, yet everyone had enough according to their needs.

Did you know? The gathering of manna teaches here that storing things out of fear is not always helpful. Food kept against the instruction spoiled, while the portion gathered on the sixth day lasted for the Sabbath.

Did you know? This chapter contains the first command to prepare the needs of the Sabbath in advance. The Sabbath is therefore presented not only as a day of rest, but also as a day prepared for beforehand.

Did you know? The description of manna combines appearance and taste: it resembled white coriander seed and tasted like a honey cake. The Bible presents it through several senses, not merely as food from heaven.

Did you know? According to the Book of Joshua, the manna stopped after the Israelites entered the land and began eating its produce. In this way, manna marks the transition from wilderness life to settled life.
